slides.title: There was a backup, but it wouldn't restore
slides.tldr: Believing your backup works is not the same as restoring it and seeing; a backup nobody has tested often turns out empty or corrupt on the day it is needed.

blocks.body: At 3:02 on a Friday afternoon, a developer runs `DELETE FROM orders` on production by mistake, without a `WHERE`. It's noticed within ten minutes. "Don't worry, we back up every night." But when they go to restore, the backup files turn out to be 0 bytes: the disk had been full for 3 weeks. Nobody ever opened a file to check.

blocks.caption: A backup ran every night, and for three weeks it was empty

actors.label: Developer
actors.tip: Made the mistake, but the real fault is in the system: data can be deleted from production this easily.

actors.label: Production DB
actors.tip: Does what it is told, even a mistaken command.

actors.label: Backup server
actors.tip: Stores a file every night, but nobody checks whether the file is any good.

messages.label: File is 0 bytes: empty for 3 weeks
messages.tip: The disk was full and the backup job failed silently. Nobody had set up an alert.

blocks.body: A backup you have never restored is not a backup. It is a hope.

aside.title: A real story, many times over
aside.body: Companies large and small have lived this: the backup job showed green, but the files were useless because of a wrong directory, a full disk or a lost password. They found out on the very day they needed them.

items.meaning: Recovery Point Objective: the most data, measured in time, you can afford to lose.
Recovery Time Objective: how quickly you must be back up and running.

check.q: Why can't you be sure the backup is fine just because the nightly job reports "success"?
check.a: A successful job only means the command finished. Whether the file is complete, intact and restorable is proven only by actually restoring it.

slides.title: Photocopies of the deed: the 3-2-1 rule
slides.tldr: Keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 kinds of storage, with 1 at another location. And a replica is not a backup, because a mistaken DELETE reaches it instantly too.

blocks.title: The house deed
blocks.body: The original deed for your house sits in the safe at home. What if it burns or gets stolen? So you keep a photocopy in a bank locker and another at your parents' house in a different city. If the house burns, the locker copy survives; if the city floods, the copy in the other city does. Keep all copies in the same safe and you really have one copy.

blocks.caption: 3-2-1: three copies, two kinds of storage, one far away

nodes.label: Production DB
nodes.tip: The live database. It counts as a copy, but isn't enough on its own.

nodes.label: Separate disk
nodes.tip: Regular backups and WAL on a separate machine or disk, for fast restores.

nodes.label: Bucket in another region
nodes.tip: Object storage in another city or region. Turn on immutability (no deletes) here.

edges.label: Daily full-incremental backups and WAL go to a separate disk
That copy goes to a bucket in another region, made immutable
WAL also goes there directly, so you can recover to the latest moment

blocks.body: A replica is not a backup. A mistaken DELETE and ransomware reach the replica instantly too.

aside.body: With a single copy, any one of fire, disk wear, a mistaken command or an attacker ends everything.

items: Turn on object lock (immutability) on the offsite bucket, so neither an attacker nor a mistake can delete the copies.
Store the backup encryption key somewhere else, or you will have the files and no way to open them.
Price: three copies cost about three times the storage, and a locked copy can't be deleted before its retention ends. Set a retention period, such as 30 days.

check.q: The primary already has a replica. Why do you still need a separate backup?
check.a: A replica copies every change from the primary the moment it happens, including a mistaken DELETE. A backup lets you go back to an earlier moment; a replica doesn't.

slides.title: Point-in-time recovery: back to one minute before the mistake
slides.tldr: A base backup plus continuously archived WAL lets you recover to any moment; the restore happens on a new server, never on top of the live DB.

blocks.body: A nightly backup is only a picture of 2 a.m.; for a mistake at 3:02 in the afternoon it loses 13 hours of data. **PITR** fixes that: PostgreSQL collects a log of every transaction (the **WAL**) in a separate place. To restore, you first lay down the nightly picture, then replay the WAL and stop at exactly 3:01 p.m. MySQL does the same with its binary log.

blocks.code:
wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-push %p'
archive_timeout = 60        # push a WAL file at least every 60 seconds

marks.tip: Every completed WAL file goes to the backup repository (ideally offsite). This is what preserves "all the writes in between".
Forces a WAL file out even if it isn't full. So the RPO is about 1 minute.

blocks.file: restore, then put the lost rows back
blocks.code:
# never on the live DB; use a new or scratch server
sudo systemctl stop postgresql
pgbackrest --stanza=main restore \
  --type=time --target='2026-11-20 15:01:00-05' \
  --target-action=promote
sudo systemctl start postgresql

psql -c 'SELECT count(*), max(created_at) FROM orders'   # check it looks right

# the lost rows go back into production through a staging table
psql -c "\copy orders TO 'orders.csv' CSV"                       # on the scratch server
psql -h prod -c 'CREATE TABLE orders_restored (LIKE orders)'
psql -h prod -c "\copy orders_restored FROM 'orders.csv' CSV"
psql -h prod -c 'INSERT INTO orders SELECT * FROM orders_restored ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING'

marks.tip: The time one minute before the mistake. Don't forget the timezone (-05) with the time.
On reaching the target, the DB comes up (promote); otherwise it sits read-only, waiting.
Finally count for yourself: are the orders back, is the latest timestamp right? This is the check before you go live.
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: orders that exist in production today stay untouched, and only the lost ones come in.

items: Do the PITR on a scratch server first, then copy only the missing data back into production. Rolling the whole DB back also loses every valid transaction made after the mistake.
Without pgBackRest, doing it by hand needs `restore_command`, `recovery_target_time` and a `recovery.signal` file.
If the backup server's clock and the DB server's time disagree, the target time lands in the wrong place.
Price: the WAL archive grows with your write volume, and replaying a whole day of WAL makes the restore longer. A fresh base backup every day keeps it short.

check.q: Even with a 2 a.m. backup, why do you need PITR?
check.a: The nightly backup restores only the 2 a.m. state, losing about 13 hours of data up to the mistake. Replaying WAL takes you to exactly one minute before it.

slides.title: Restore drills: break it yourself and see
slides.tldr: Once a week, restore the latest backup into a scratch DB, time it and verify the data; alert immediately if it fails.

blocks.body: A backup is trustworthy only when a machine restores it by itself once a week. This command restores the latest backup into a scratch DB, starts it, measures how long it took (that is your real **RTO**), and runs a few sanity checks: are there enough orders, and is the newest data recent?

marks.tip: Runs by itself every Sunday at 5 a.m. Nobody has to remember.
`mustRun()` throws if it fails; the scheduler logs the failure, so you get an alert.
The restored copy inherits the live archive settings. Switch archiving off, or the scratch server pushes WAL into the real backup repository.
Just "the restore ran" isn't enough. Checking that the data is complete and recent is what catches an empty backup.
Chart the measured time. As the data grows the restore slows down, and the RTO quietly creeps up.

blocks.caption: How restore time (minutes) grows as the data grows

items.label: Last year
items.tip: With a small database the restore was fast, so the RTO was never a worry.

items.label: Now
items.tip: The data grew and the restore got slower. Nobody noticed.

items.label: Target RTO
items.tip: The business can accept at most one hour of downtime. Today's 70 minutes is over that.

items: Write the time the drill measures into the runbook as the "expected duration".
The scratch DB holds personal data; protect it like production, and delete it when the job is done.
Price: the scratch server needs as much disk as production and runs for the whole restore. That is cheap next to finding out on the day of the disaster.

check.q: Besides "the file restored", which two data checks does a restore drill need, and why?
check.a: That there are enough orders, and that the newest data is recent. Those two catch an empty or stale backup, which can still restore without any error.

slides.title: The runbook: the page you read when you're scared
slides.tldr: A runbook is step-by-step instructions you can follow half asleep: who does what, which commands, how to verify, and it is updated after every drill.

blocks.body: At 3 a.m., in a crisis, your head doesn't work. What you need is a page where every step is simple enough for a half-asleep person. That is a **runbook**: who to call, which command, what you should see if it worked, what you should see if you must stop. In an emergency you don't make a plan; you follow the written one.

blocks.code:
RUNBOOK: Production DB restore (PITR)
Owner: data team · last drill: 2026-11-15 (70 minutes)

When: mistaken DELETE/UPDATE, disk failure, suspected ransomware

1. Open an incident channel, pick an incident commander
2. Stop writes: `php bin/console app:maintenance on`
3. Note the exact time of the mistake (from the logs) → T
4. Restore on a new server: target 1 minute before T
   pgbackrest --stanza=main restore --type=time \
     --target='T' --target-action=promote
5. Verify: `psql -c 'SELECT count(*), max(created_at) FROM orders'`
   Expect: order count ≈ yesterday's, max(created_at) ≈ T
6. Copy the deleted rows back via a staging table (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING)
   (don't swap the whole DB: valid transactions came after the mistake)
7. Maintenance off, watch for 1 hour, write the post-mortem

Stop if: the restore runs past 120 minutes → phone the data lead

marks.tip: With the date and duration of the last drill written down, you know how old the page is and how long this will take.
Commands are written out exactly, ready to copy and paste. Nobody types from memory in a crisis.
Next to each step is what "correct" looks like. It stops you heading down the wrong path.
Not a whole-DB rollback; you would lose the valid transactions that came after the mistake.

blocks.title: Five qualities of a good runbook
items: Every step is short, in order and copy-pastable.
Next to each step is what "correct" looks like.
It names the owner and when the last drill was.
It is clear when to stop and whom to call.
It is updated after every drill or incident.

blocks.body: At 3 a.m. you can't invent a plan. You can follow a written one.

aside.body: An outdated runbook is a wrong one. Read it at every drill and replace stale steps.

check.q: Why is it important to write "what correct looks like" next to each runbook step?
check.a: When you're frightened you can take a wrong step without noticing. With the expected result written down, you know at once whether you are on the right path.

slides.title: Fixed it, so replay everything: and the second disaster
slides.tldr: Replaying 4000 failed events in one go causes double processing and overloads your own systems; the recovery itself becomes a second incident.

blocks.body: For 6 hours a bug made the payment webhook handler fail, and 4000 events piled up. The bug was fixed, and an engineer ran a one-line script: push every event back onto the queue. Of those 4000, 600 had been partly processed already (the money was credited, then the receipt step failed), and they credited money a second time. And 4000 jobs at once is 6 hours of traffic in one go, so the database and the gateway buckled.

blocks.caption: The attempt to fix things became a second disaster

actors.label: Engineer
actors.tip: Ran the script with good intentions, but with no limit, no rehearsal and no safety net.

actors.label: Queue
actors.tip: Accepts whatever arrives, even 4000 jobs at once.

actors.label: DB and gateway
actors.tip: Not built to take this much pressure all at once.

messages.tip: On an already slow system, new retries add even more load.
This happened because events already partly processed ran a second time.

blocks.body: A replay is not new work, it is old work done again. So it must be idempotent, slow and rehearsed first.

aside.body: You have no choice but to run failed work again, but done carelessly it causes a bigger disaster than the original one.

items.meaning: Running events or jobs again that failed or were lost earlier.

check.q: Why were 600 events processed twice in the replay?
check.a: They had already been partly processed, and the handler had no way of knowing which. With no idempotent guard, it did the work a second time.

slides.title: The backlog of letters: four safeguards
slides.tldr: Four safeguards for a safe replay: an idempotent handler, a throttle, a dry run and a checkpoint. All four, together.

blocks.title: The mail backlog after a postal strike
blocks.body: After a strike, 3,000 letters have piled up at the post office. The postman first counts the list (dry run). He checks each letter's receipt and doesn't deliver again if it was already delivered (idempotent). He delivers 300 a day on top of the normal post, so the office keeps running (throttle). And he marks the bundle "done up to here" (checkpoint), so if he falls ill, someone else can pick up from that point.

blocks.caption: The four safeguards: what each prevents, and how

rows.tip: The handler itself remembers which events it has already handled, and does nothing when one arrives again.
A pace at which the system can handle normal work and the recovery together.
Says how many jobs would run and which ones, without running anything. A wrong filter gets caught early.

cells: Starting over after a mid-run stop
Save the last id, resume from it
rows.tip: If the command crashes or is stopped, the next run picks up where it left off.

blocks.body: Count before you run. Run slowly. If you stop, resume where you stopped.

aside.body: Count, look, run slowly, mark the spot.

items.meaning: A saved marker of how far the work has got, such as the last processed id.
A rehearsal of the whole job that changes nothing real and just shows the result.

check.q: How do a dry run and a checkpoint do different jobs?
check.a: A dry run catches mistakes before running (how many, which ones). A checkpoint remembers where to resume if you stop partway through.

slides.title: A Symfony console command: slowly, with a bookmark
slides.tldr: A console command with `--dry-run`, `--rate` and a checkpoint: it takes events in batches, dispatches slowly and saves the last id after each batch.

blocks.body: Don't load the whole list into memory. Fetch batches of 100, and instead of `OFFSET`, fetch from just after the last id (**keyset pagination**). Save a checkpoint at the end of each batch. With `--dry-run`, skip both the dispatch and the checkpoint. At 20 a second, 4000 events take about 3 minutes: slow for a computer, still quick for a recovery.

marks.tip: With `--dry-run` nothing is dispatched; it only counts how many jobs there would be.
Starts from wherever the previous run stopped. 0 the first time.
Replay work goes to its own `replay` transport, so a few workers there can be limited apart from normal work.
A pause after every dispatch. At 20 per second, that is 50,000 microseconds.
A marker after each batch. If the command crashes, at most one batch repeats, and since the handler is idempotent, no harm is done.

blocks.file: migrations: checkpoint and the next batch

marks.tip: One row per job. Saving again and again just updates that same row.
`id > :after` jumps straight there through the index. With a large OFFSET the database must skip every earlier row each time, which is slow.

items.desc: a limited worker on a separate transport

items: Send replay work to its own `replay` transport and run few workers there, so normal work isn't slowed down.
Don't just raise the rate. Raise it while watching the dashboard, and only if CPU, DB connections and error rate stay normal.

check.q: Why use `id > :after` instead of `OFFSET` to fetch the batches of 100?
check.a: With a large OFFSET, the database must skip all the earlier rows every time, which is slow. `id > :after` jumps straight there through the index, and it matches the checkpoint too.

slides.title: Run twice, nothing doubles: and no receipt goes missing
slides.tldr: Make the replay handler idempotent, and queue each outside side effect once in a table, so a replay neither doubles it nor skips one the first attempt missed.

blocks.body: The most dangerous handler is one that does its work every time it runs, so the handler remembers which events it has already handled. Work that leaves your system (an email, an SMS) can't be taken back, so the replay never sends it directly. It writes one "send this receipt" row per event, with a UNIQUE `event_id`, and a separate sender emails each unsent row once. Why not just a "skip emails during a replay" switch? Some of the 600 events were credited and then failed before the receipt. The switch would skip the credit (right) and the receipt (wrong): those customers would never get one.

marks.tip: Nobody checks whether this event was processed before. The second time, the money is credited again.
The customer gets the email again. A sent email can't be recalled.
Guard 1: the event_id INSERT and the credit share one transaction. Either both happen or neither does.
0 rows means this event was already credited. Skip the credit, but not the receipt row below.
Guard 2: its own unique key. It runs even when the credit was done earlier, so a receipt the first attempt missed is queued now.

blocks.caption: How each kind of work should behave in a replay

rows.tip: Writes to the ledger or wallet must be idempotent. This is the main protection.
Once it has gone out it can't be recalled. A unique row sends it once, and also covers events the first attempt missed.
Send the original transaction's key again, so the other side also treats it as one.

cells: As many times as you like
rows.tip: These are "set" operations by nature, so running twice gives the same result.

items: Events handled before the guard existed have no `processed_event` row, so a replay would credit them again. Backfill rows for events that already have a ledger credit, and check the count in the dry run.
Don't trust an old event's payload to reverse today's state. Decide by looking at the current state.

check.q: The credit was already done by the first attempt. Why does the replay still insert the receipt row?
check.a: The first attempt may have failed before the receipt. The row's own unique key queues it once: no duplicate if it was sent, and no missing receipt if it wasn't.

slides.title: Sending each receipt once, missed ones included
slides.tldr: A separate sender emails the unsent receipt rows in small batches and marks each one sent, so every event ends with exactly one receipt.

blocks.body: The replay only fills the `receipt_outbox` table. A small periodic job does the emailing. Three kinds of event can meet a replay, and each one ends with exactly one receipt.

blocks.caption: What the replay does for each kind of event

rows.tip: Both guards say done, and the customer already has the receipt.
The case a plain "skip emails in a replay" switch would lose.
Both guards pass, so the replay does the full job once.

marks.tip: Only unsent rows, 50 at a time, every 10 seconds. A backlog of 600 receipts drains in about 2 minutes, with no flood of email.
Sent first, marked second. A crash between the two lines means one duplicate email, never a missing one.

items: Price: that rare duplicate is fine for a receipt, never for money. Money keeps its own guard.
Keep the rows. `sent_at` is also your proof that the receipt went out.

items.meaning: A table of "things still to send". One writer fills it safely, and one sender empties it.

check.q: A customer was credited, but the first attempt failed before the receipt. What does the replay do for them?
check.a: The credit guard skips the credit. The receipt insert adds the missing row, and the sender emails it once.

slides.title: A silent UPDATE in production: a fix that makes things worse
slides.tldr: Seeing bad data and hurriedly running an UPDATE in the console leaves no evidence, can change the wrong rows, and later nobody can tell what happened.

blocks.body: A bad deploy wrongly marked 2300 paid orders as `canceled` within two hours. In a hurry, an engineer ran `UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE status = 'canceled'` in the production console. The 2300 were fixed, but 12,000 older orders that really had been canceled over the past months also became `paid`. Nobody wrote down which rows changed.

blocks.caption: A one-line UPDATE, with no evidence left behind

actors.label: Bad deploy
actors.tip: The new code had a bug that wrongly canceled paid orders.

actors.label: Engineer
actors.tip: Wants to fix it fast, with good intentions. But in the rush the condition grew too broad.

actors.label: Production DB
actors.tip: Does what it is told. Can't tell which rows are the right ones and which are wrong.

messages.label: UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'canceled'
messages.tip: The condition has no time window and no check for a paid payment.
The 12,000 orders that really were canceled are now marked paid too. They might even get shipped.

messages.note: The old values are written nowhere
messages.tip: Now there is no way to tell what each row held before.

blocks.body: A correction is a transaction too. Who, when, why, and what it was before: all of it gets written down.

aside.title: Two weeks later
aside.body: The accounts team saw that the payment and order counts didn't match. Nobody could say who had changed what, or why. The console command left no log, and the values before the change were gone.
Correcting bad data is unavoidable. The question is how, so that the correction itself can be understood and reversed later.

check.q: Why did that UPDATE change 12,000 wrong rows as well?
check.a: The condition was just `status = canceled`. With no time window for the bad deploy and no check for a paid payment, orders that were genuinely canceled matched too.

slides.title: Corrections in red ink: four ways to fix data
slides.tldr: Fix by writing, not erasing: a reversing and a new entry in the ledger, a rule-following transition for state, a recompute for derived data, and an audited script for the rest.

blocks.title: Red ink in the store's account book
blocks.body: When a wrong amount is written in the ledger, a good bookkeeper doesn't rub it out. He writes a line in red ink, "wrong amount canceled", then a new line with the correct amount below it, with the date and his name. Both the original mistake and the correction stay visible. This is exactly how data corrections should work in software.

blocks.caption: How to fix each kind of data

rows.tip: A money entry never changes. You write the opposite transaction to cancel its effect, then post the correct one.

cells: Keeps when and why it changed
rows.tip: Don't just set the status. Changing it through a valid path builds a history with reasons.
Never hand-edit a derived value; calculate it again from the entries.
The before and after of every row sits in the log, so the whole fix can be reversed if needed.

blocks.caption: A deposit posted as $5,000 instead of $500, fixed in red ink

rows.tip: The original wrong posting. It is never edited or deleted.
The same two accounts, on opposite sides, so its effect cancels E-1 exactly.
The deposit as it should have been posted in the first place.
Add the three entries: $500 in, with both sides equal, and the whole story still visible.

blocks.body: Fix by writing, not erasing: the mistake stays and so does the correction.

items.meaning: An opposite action that cancels the effect of an earlier one, rather than erasing it.
A one-off, documented job that corrects wrong production data.

items: Price: a correction takes two or three rows instead of one UPDATE, and queries must count the reversal pairs. That price buys the audit trail.
Reversing entries are for money. For an address or a profile, an audited script is enough.

check.q: If a ledger holds an entry with a wrong amount, what is the right way to fix it, and why?
check.a: Write a reversing entry to cancel the mistake's effect, then write a new entry with the correct amount. History stays intact and debit = credit still holds.

slides.title: An audited data-fix script: count, record, then change
slides.tldr: A narrow condition, a check against the expected count, one transaction, each row's before and after in data_fix_log, and nothing changing if you run it again.

blocks.body: Instead of a hand-typed UPDATE in the console, write a small script named after the ticket number. First it counts how many rows would change. If that doesn't match your "expected count", it stops. If it does, it changes the rows in one transaction and writes each row's before and after values to a log. The condition should be such that running it again finds 0 rows.

blocks.code:
WITH bad AS (
  SELECT o.id, o.status AS old_status
    FROM orders o
   WHERE o.updated_at >= '2026-11-20 13:00-05'
     AND o.updated_at <  '2026-11-20 15:05-05'    -- window of the bad deploy
     AND o.status = 'canceled'
     AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payment p
                  WHERE p.order_id = o.id AND p.status = 'paid')
     FOR UPDATE OF o
), fixed AS (
  UPDATE orders o SET status = 'paid', updated_at = now()
    FROM bad WHERE o.id = bad.id
  RETURNING o.id, bad.old_status, o.status AS new_status
)
INSERT INTO data_fix_log (fix_id, row_id, old_value, new_value)
SELECT 'FIX-1042', id, old_status, new_status FROM fixed;

-- undo FIX-1042 from its log, if it turns out to be wrong
UPDATE orders o SET status = l.old_value
  FROM data_fix_log l
 WHERE l.fix_id = 'FIX-1042' AND l.row_id = o.id
   AND o.status = l.new_value;

marks.tip: Only rows inside the bad deploy's time window. Genuinely canceled orders from before or after are left alone.
Needs proof: this order really has a paid payment. The narrower the condition, the less room for error.
The UPDATE and the log are in one statement. A change without a log entry simply can't happen.
Each row's before and after values are written. If needed, the fix can be reversed from this.
Only rows still in the state the fix left them are put back. A row someone changed since is left alone.
If the counted number doesn't match the expected one, nothing changes. A wrong condition, or surprising data, is caught right here.
`--dry-run` only shows the number. A second person looks at this output and signs off.
Run it again and it finds 0 rows. `status = canceled` no longer matches, so a double fix can't happen.

items: Put the script through code review and attach the dry-run output to the ticket. Nothing goes into production without a second pair of eyes.
Take a snapshot of the affected rows before running; `data_fix_log` gives you a way to undo, and the backup is the last resort.
Price: review and a dry run add some time, often under an hour. A second wrong fix costs far more than that hour.
A data-fix script must never change a ledger money entry. Money mistakes are always fixed with a reversing entry.

check.q: Why does the script change nothing when run again, and why is that good?
check.a: After the fix, the condition `status = canceled` no longer matches, so it finds 0 rows. Running it twice by mistake, or again after a crash, is safe.

slides.title: Code rolls back, data doesn't: roll back or roll forward
slides.tldr: Rolling back restores code quickly but not the data the bad code wrote; when the schema or data has changed, roll forward plus a data fix is the way.

blocks.body: When a curry has too much salt, you have two options: throw the whole pot away and cook it again (roll back), or rescue it with potato and water (roll forward). A bad deploy is the same. But one thing is always true: even after the code goes back to the earlier version, the data the bad code already wrote doesn't fix itself.

blocks.caption: The two paths, and when to use which

columns.title: Roll back
items: The code changed, not the schema or data
Fast and simple: put the old version back
Risk: bad data already written stays
columns.tip: Go back to the previous version. Fast, when data and schema haven't changed.

columns.title: Roll forward
items: A new column or data is already live
The fix is small and tested, the pipeline fast
Plus an audited data fix for the bad data
Risk: a rushed fix can bring a second bug
columns.tip: Deploy a small fix and move ahead. For when going back is impossible or risky.

blocks.code:
# roll back: go to the previous version (the schema does not go back!)
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api

# roll forward: revert the bad commit and deploy again
git revert --no-edit 4f2a9c1 && git push origin main

# on either path, next: find the affected data and run an audited fix
php bin/console app:fix:1042 --dry-run --expect=2300

marks.tip: The code goes back. But if a migration dropped a column, the old code won't run without it.
Whichever path you take, the bad data is still in the database. That is a separate job.

blocks.body: Rolling back the code doesn't roll back the data the bad code wrote. That needs its own documented fix.

use: Roll back: only code changed, with no data change or destructive migration
Roll forward: data is already written in the new shape, or the fix is small and safe
avoid: Rolling back code after a migration has dropped a column

check.q: After the roll back, 2300 orders were still canceled. Why, and what is the next step?
check.a: A roll back restores only the code; the bad code had already changed the data. Next, run an audited data-fix script with a narrow condition to correct those rows.
